Thanks. I found Q3 quite tricky – drawing a line between helpful data and overreach felt subjective. Specifically with Absalon data (Q3.4), even a ‘small’ improvement feels like it might not justify tracking *how* students use the learning platform.

For me, questions around explainability (Q4) are most crucial. As someone who restarted a master's, I know feeling understood is vital for support to be effective. 

I was surprised by the strong consensus on accepting a 5% accuracy loss for fairness (Q5.1). I’m glad of it, but wonder if some might underestimate what that represents in terms of missed students. Perhaps an opt-out mechanism could alleviate concerns about data use without sacrificing fairness?

Thanks. I agree with S8 – Q3 felt like a slippery slope. Especially around Absalon data; while *a* small improvement sounds okay on paper, tracking online behaviour feels intrusive and presumes engagement equals progress. For me, that’s too far.

I think the questions about explainability (Q4) are absolutely vital. As someone managing a long-term health condition impacting my studies, I need to understand *why* anything is flagged – it's about trust and feeling supported, not just labelled. 

I was also a bit surprised by the strong support for accepting even a small loss in accuracy for fairness (Q5.1). While I agree with that principle, it reinforces the need for an opt-out; students should have agency over their data and how it’s used, even if it slightly impacts model performance.

Thanks to both S8 and S9 – I completely agree with a lot of what you said. Q3 *was* difficult; it felt like an endless series of “what ifs” where the benefit wasn’t always clear against the privacy implications. The Absalon data especially gave me pause – tracking behaviour feels… reductive, and assumes correlation equals causation.

I think explainability (Q4) is paramount. As a student with a disability who's *used* support services, I know that feeling understood is key. A model flagging me without explanation wouldn’t be helpful; it would feel disempowering. 

While I answered 'small' for using disability data if it improved identification (Q3.5), and accept the loss in accuracy for fairness (Q5.1) – both are conditional on a *robust* opt-out, and transparent data handling. Agency is non-negotiable.

Thanks to S3, S8, and S9 – I echo a lot of those sentiments. Q3 felt like navigating a minefield; incremental additions sound harmless until you consider the cumulative effect on privacy. The Absalon data particularly worries me as an advisor; simply *being* online doesn’t equate to engagement or understanding material.

I think explainability (Q4) is absolutely critical, especially when dealing with vulnerable students. As an advisor for 11 years, I know building rapport and trust requires transparency. Knowing *why* a student is flagged allows me to tailor support effectively.

While I answered “small” on several of the data additions, it’s predicated on rigorous safeguards and – crucially – a clear opt-out mechanism. Agency is paramount, even if it means slightly less accurate predictions. We need to build trust, not surveillance.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 really difficult too – especially thinking about Absalon data. It feels like it moves beyond identifying *difficulties* and starts to judge *how* someone studies, which isn’t fair. As someone who had to restart a program, I know life throws things at you, and sometimes study habits change because of that, not necessarily because you're failing.

For me, Q4 is hugely important. Knowing *why* I’m flagged feels vital. Explainability builds trust, and helps me understand what support would actually be useful. 

I agree with the strong feeling about fairness (Q5). While a small loss of accuracy might seem okay, it highlights why that opt-out is so crucial – students need control over their data. It’s easy to imagine someone feeling labelled, even if flagged accurately.

Thanks everyone. I also found Q3 quite challenging – especially balancing potential benefit with privacy. As an international student still adjusting to this system, I’m particularly sensitive about data collection. While course performance feels reasonable, adding Absalon data felt like a step too far; it doesn't account for different learning styles or cultural approaches to study.

I strongly agree explainability (Q4) is vital. Understanding *why* I was flagged would be crucial for me to trust any support offered. The 5% accuracy loss for fairness (Q5.1) feels right, but absolutely requires a clear opt-out. Being new to the country and the university system, maintaining control over my data feels especially important while I’m learning how things work here.

Thanks everyone – I agree with much of what’s been said already. Q3 was definitely tricky; that incremental creep felt significant, and Absalon data does raise concerns about judging *how* students learn rather than simply *if* they're struggling. As an advisor for six years, I see the nuances daily.

For me, questions around explainability (Q4) are paramount. We need to be able to articulate *why* a student is flagged – not just to build trust with them, but also so *we*, as advisors, can effectively tailor our support. 

I answered 'small' on many of the data additions, conditional on a robust opt-out and transparency. A loss of 5% accuracy for fairness (Q5) feels reasonable if it ensures equitable outcomes, but student agency must be central to this process.

Thanks everyone – I really appreciate hearing those perspectives, especially from the advisors. Q3 definitely felt like a balancing act, and I agree with S8 and others about Absalon data; tracking behaviour feels… intrusive. As someone with ADHD who’s restarted a program, my study patterns aren't always ‘typical’, and that shouldn’t be penalised.

For me, explainability (Q4) is *hugely* important – feeling understood is key after dropping out once before. The 5% loss for fairness (Q5.1) feels right, but only with a solid opt-out. I need to feel in control of my data, especially given my previous experiences. It’s about trusting the system won’t just label me, but genuinely support *me*.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 really difficult – especially thinking about adding things like Absalon data. It feels a bit…presumptuous to assume how someone uses a platform reflects whether they’re struggling. As someone with dyslexia and needing extra time, my online activity might look different.

I think explainability (Q4) is vital. Knowing *why* I was flagged would be key for me to actually engage with support. The 5% loss of accuracy for fairness feels right, but that opt-out is absolutely non-negotiable. Being a first-year student, I’m still figuring things out and want control over my data while I adjust. Transparency builds trust – and as someone who's struggled before, that matters hugely.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said, especially around Q3 and Absalon data – it feels like it moves from identifying difficulties to judging study *style*. As someone who moved countries and is still learning Danish, my online behaviour might be different just because of that adjustment, not necessarily because I'm struggling.

I think explainability (Q4) is so important, having dropped out once before. Understanding *why* I was flagged would make me much more likely to seek help. Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what's been said, especially concerning Q3 and that incremental creep of data collection. As an advisor, I see students *already* feeling surveilled by administrative processes – adding more data feels like it reinforces that anxiety. Absalon data feels particularly problematic; engagement doesn’t equal understanding, and different students learn differently.

For me, explainability (Q4) is paramount. We need to be able to clearly articulate *why* a student is flagged to build trust and tailor support effectively. The 5% accuracy loss for fairness (Q5) feels acceptable *only* with that robust opt-out we’ve all mentioned. Ultimately, agency and transparency are key – students deserve control over their data and how it's used to support them.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – Q3 felt like a slippery slope, and Absalon data definitely raised red flags for me. As an international student still adapting, being tracked feels especially intrusive.

For me, explainability (Q4) is vital. Understanding *why* the model flagged me would be crucial to trust any support offered.
